title: BlackTech
summary: BlackTech is a long running intrusion cluster that public reporting describes as suspected Chinese cyber espionage, catalogued in MITRE ATT&CK as group G0098. Reporting collected there describes sustained targeting of organisations in East Asia, particularly Taiwan, Japan and Hong Kong, as well as victims in the United States, with activity tracked from at least 2013. The victim set reported is mostly media, construction, engineering, electronics and finance, which reflects an interest in industrial and intellectual property rather than in payment systems. Tradecraft blends bespoke malware with dual use administration tools. The group has been reported using exploits against internet facing services, including an old buffer overflow in a web server component, to turn a compromised host into an attacker controlled web or command server of its own. Phishing with password protected archives and documents that rely on the user enabling macros is a recurring delivery route, and the reported tooling includes remote control and downloader families alongside ordinary utilities for remote access and remote execution. Reporting also describes the use of valid digital certificates obtained from compromise rather than issued legitimately, which weakens the assumption that a signed binary is trustworthy. Evidence tends to accumulate on servers rather than endpoints: web server logs showing exploit attempts and unusual requests, unexpected files in web directories, and outbound connections from servers that have no business talking to the internet. A frequent misunderstanding is to treat a signed file or a familiar utility name as proof of safety; both were borrowed from the environment in these reports.

beginner.definition: BlackTech is the name for a group of intruders that public reports link to China. Researchers have watched it attack companies and government offices in East Asia since about 2013. It uses both its own harmful software and normal admin tools. Its targets are often media, building, electronics and finance companies.
beginner.whyItMatters: The group goes after useful information, such as designs, plans and business secrets. It often breaks in through old internet facing servers that nobody patched. It also sends emails with harmful attachments that look like ordinary business files. Because it uses everyday tools after breaking in, its actions look like normal admin work. If you only trust the tool name in your logs, you will miss it.
howItWorks: The group looks for an internet facing server that runs old, unpatched software.
It exploits a known weakness in that software so its own code runs on the server.
From that server it sends phishing email with harmful archives or documents attached.
A person opens the file, allows macros, and runs the hidden code on their own computer.
The intruders then use remote access and remote execution tools to move around the network.
They hide harmful files behind names that look like trusted programs and use stolen certificates.
beginner.example: Think of a delivery driver who wears a real courier company uniform. The uniform is genuine, but the driver no longer works for that company. Guards at the gate wave the van through because the uniform and the clipboard look right. Inside, the driver walks to the storeroom, takes what was meant to be protected, and leaves through the same gate. Nobody checks the identity, only the appearance. This is how borrowed certificates and copied tool names work online. A valid signature proves that a file was signed with some key, not that the person holding the key meant you well.
takeaways: A valid digital signature does not prove a file is safe to run.
Old internet facing servers are the front door these intruders prefer.
Watch for files and tools on servers that nobody on your team installed.

objectives: Describe BlackTech and the sectors and regions that public reporting associates with it.
Explain how exploitation of an internet facing server can create attacker controlled web infrastructure.
Recognise why stolen code signing certificates undermine trust decisions based on file signatures.
Identify server side log and file system evidence that suggests an intrusion through a web facing service.
Explain why the presence of a legitimate administration tool in logs is not by itself proof of legitimate activity.
